title: Polar Night
theme: Advanced tooling, resilience and cleanup for the long dark

missions.title: Don't Download Twice
missions.story:
**From:** Amara Okafor
**Subject:** climate-fetch rebuilds are eating the satellite budget

Every time I touch one line of `requirements.txt`, pip downloads every package again. The Dockerfile even has `--no-cache-dir` in it, because someone once told me that keeps images small. Ten rebuilds a day over a metered link adds up fast.

Can you make the build keep pip's download cache between builds, without baking the cache into the image? Build the result as `kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0`.
objectives: Edit `/workspace/Dockerfile` so the pip install step uses a BuildKit cache mount on `/root/.cache/pip`
Remove `--no-cache-dir` from the install step
Build the image as `kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0`; it must still run and print `climate-fetch ready`
missions.startingState: `/workspace` holds a working Dockerfile, `requirements.txt` and `fetch.py` for the climate-fetch tool, but nothing has been built yet.
hints: The build engine (BuildKit) can mount a directory that persists between builds but never becomes part of an image layer. That is exactly what a package manager's download cache needs.
Attach it to the install step with `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=DIR ...`. pip's cache lives in `/root/.cache/pip`, and `--no-cache-dir` would tell pip to ignore it, so it has to go.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]
```
Then `docker build -t kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0 .`

files.content:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]

validation.description: The Dockerfile installs with `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip` and without `--no-cache-dir`
The image `kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0` exists
`kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0` runs and prints `climate-fetch ready`

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]
EOF
missions.debrief: The second build skipped the download because the cache mount survived between builds, and it never became part of a layer, so the image stays lean. Pro tip: the same trick works for `apk` (`/var/cache/apk`), Go (`/root/.cache/go-build`) and `npm`.

missions.title: Whisper to the Builder
missions.story:
Excerpt from the mainland's image-scan report on `kestrel/uplink:0.9`:

`FINDING HIGH  layer 2  ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN=KP-4e9b... is readable with docker history`

The uplink build has to prove it can authenticate, so it really does need the mainland token while it builds. But the token must not survive in any layer, environment variable or history line. The token file is `/workspace/secrets/mainland.token`.

Rewrite the Dockerfile so BuildKit hands the token over as a secret, and build `kestrel/uplink:1.0`.
objectives: Rewrite `/workspace/Dockerfile` to read the token through `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token` and drop the `ARG`
Build `kestrel/uplink:1.0` passing `secrets/mainland.token` as the secret `mainland_token`
The build still wrote `token-ok` to `/opt/uplink-status`, but the token appears nowhere in the image or its history
missions.startingState: `/workspace/Dockerfile` is the leaky version that takes the token as `ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN`; `/workspace/secrets/mainland.token` holds the token. No image has been built.
hints: Build arguments and environment variables are recorded in image metadata forever. BuildKit has a different channel: a secret is mounted for a single `RUN` step as a temporary file and leaves no trace.

In the Dockerfile, add `--mount=type=secret,id=NAME` to the `RUN` that needs it; the value appears as the file `/run/secrets/NAME`. At build time supply it with `docker build --secret id=NAME,src=FILE`.

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token \
    grep -q '^KP-' /run/secrets/mainland_token \
    && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]
```
```bash
docker build -t kestrel/uplink:1.0 \
  --secret id=mainland_token,src=secrets/mainland.token .
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN
RUN echo "$MAINLAND_TOKEN" | grep -q '^KP-' && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]

validation.description: The Dockerfile uses `--mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token` and no longer declares `ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN`
The image `kestrel/uplink:1.0` exists
The build consumed the token: `/opt/uplink-status` in the image contains `token-ok`
The token does not appear in `docker history --no-trunc kestrel/uplink:1.0`

params.command: if docker image inspect kestrel/uplink:1.0 | grep -q KP-4e9b27d1- || docker run --rm --entrypoint sh kestrel/uplink:1.0 -c 'grep -rsq KP-4e9b27d1- /etc /opt /root /home /tmp /var /usr /app'; then echo LEAK; else echo CLEAN; fi

validation.description: The token is not stored in the image metadata (env, labels) or anywhere in its filesystem

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token \
    grep -q '^KP-' /run/secrets/mainland_token \
    && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]
EOF
missions.debrief: A `--build-arg` or `ENV` is written into the image for everyone who can pull it, while a secret mount exists only for the one `RUN` step that asks for it. Pro tip: `--secret id=x,env=VAR` reads the secret from an environment variable instead of a file.

missions.title: A Graceful Goodbye
missions.story:
NORA: `TIDE-LOGGER STOP TOOK 10.0 S. EXIT CODE 137. LAST FLUSH: NEVER. ORPHANED PROCESSES: 41.`

The tide logger keeps its readings in memory and only writes them out when it receives SIGINT. Docker's default stop sends SIGTERM, which the logger ignores, so after ten seconds the engine kills it and a night of readings is lost. It also leaves defunct child processes behind, because nothing reaps them.

Replace the running `tide-logger` container: give it a proper init process, SIGINT as its stop signal, and a 20-second grace period.
objectives: Remove the old `tide-logger` container and run a new detached `tide-logger` from `kestrel/tide-logger:1.0`
Run it with Docker's built-in init process (`--init`)
Stop signal `SIGINT`, grace period of `20` seconds before the kill
missions.startingState: The image `kestrel/tide-logger:1.0` is built and a naive container `tide-logger` is running from it with default settings.
hints: Two separate problems: the process at PID 1 does not forward or reap anything, and `docker stop` sends a signal the application does not handle. Both are fixed with options on the container, no code changes.

`--init` puts a tiny init program at PID 1. `--stop-signal SIGINT` changes the signal `docker stop` sends, and `--stop-timeout SECONDS` changes how long it waits before SIGKILL. These are `docker run` flags, so the old container has to be replaced.

```bash
docker rm -f tide-logger
docker run -d --name tide-logger \
  --init \
  --stop-signal SIGINT \
  --stop-timeout 20 \
  kestrel/tide-logger:1.0

docker stop tide-logger && docker logs tide-logger | tail -2
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY logger.sh /logger.sh
RUN chmod +x /logger.sh
CMD ["/logger.sh"]

#!/bin/sh
buf=0
flush() { echo "FLUSHED $buf readings"; exit 0; }
trap flush INT
echo "tide-logger started"
while true; do
  buf=$((buf + 1))
  ( sleep 1 & )
  sleep 1
done

validation.description: Container `tide-logger` is running from `kestrel/tide-logger:1.0`
`tide-logger` runs with an init process (`--init`)
`tide-logger` has the stop signal `SIGINT`
`tide-logger` has a stop timeout of 20 seconds
PID 1 inside `tide-logger` is the init process, not the logger script

missions.debrief: `docker stop` is a polite request (the stop signal) followed by a deadline (the timeout); if your program answers to a different signal, change the request rather than the program. Pro tip: put `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT` in the Dockerfile to make the right signal the image's default.

missions.title: The Other Station
missions.story:
Ingrid, on the handheld radio, voice thin against the wind:

"Engineer, the hut at Skua Ridge keeps a second Docker engine as our fallback. When we need it, it will be midnight and somebody will be typing endpoints from memory. I don't want that. Give the hut a name the CLI understands, and prove the name works by starting a probe container there. The cable isn't laid yet, so for now point it at the endpoint in `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt`. Over."
objectives: Create a context named `backup-station` for the endpoint in `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt`, with the description `Backup hut engine`
Make `backup-station` the active context with `docker context use`
Through that context, run a detached `hut-probe` container from `alpine:3.20` that sleeps (`sleep infinity`)
missions.startingState: Only the `default` context exists. The file `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt` holds the endpoint to use.
hints: The Docker CLI can talk to several engines. A context bundles an endpoint with a name, so switching engines is one short command instead of environment variables or long flags.
Create it with `docker context create NAME --docker host=ENDPOINT --description TEXT`, then switch to it with `docker context use NAME`. `docker context ls` marks the active one with an asterisk.

```bash
docker context create backup-station \
  --docker host=$(cat hut-endpoint.txt) \
  --description "Backup hut engine"
docker context use backup-station
docker context show
docker run -d --name hut-probe alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
```

validation.description: A context `backup-station` exists and points at `unix:///var/run/docker.sock`
The context `backup-station` has the description `Backup hut engine`
`backup-station` is the active context (`docker context use backup-station`)
Container `hut-probe` is running from `alpine:3.20`

solution: docker context create backup-station --docker host=unix:///var/run/docker.sock --description 'Backup hut engine'
docker run -d --name hut-probe alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: Switching engines is now one word instead of a remembered socket path: the context bundles endpoint and description under a name. Pro tip: `docker --context NAME ps` runs a single command elsewhere without changing the active context.

missions.title: A Swarm in the Dark
missions.story:
The aurora forecast printout on the corkboard has a circled line in Tomasz's tidy handwriting:

`KP index 8 tonight. Expect every screen on the station, plus the mainland, on the aurora page.`

Beneath it Ingrid has added, in pen: "One container will fall over. Three copies, spread by the engine, one front door for all of them. Use swarm."

Turn this engine into a swarm and publish the `aurora-feed` service on port 8090, with three replicas of `nginx:alpine`.
objectives: Initialise Docker Swarm on this engine
Create the service `aurora-feed` from `nginx:alpine` with `3` replicas
Publish host port `8090` to container port `80` through the service
All three replicas are running and `http://localhost:8090` answers
missions.startingState: A plain engine, not part of any swarm. `nginx:alpine` is already on the machine.
hints: Swarm mode turns one engine into a cluster manager that schedules services rather than single containers. You first switch the mode on, and then describe the service you want kept alive.

`docker swarm init` enables it (add `--advertise-addr 127.0.0.1` if Docker complains about several addresses). Then `docker service create --name NAME --replicas N -p HOST:CONTAINER IMAGE`. `--detach=false` makes the command wait for convergence.

```bash
docker swarm init
docker service create --detach=false \
  --name aurora-feed \
  --replicas 3 \
  -p 8090:80 \
  nginx:alpine
docker service ls
```

validation.description: Swarm mode is active on this engine
Service `aurora-feed` has 3 replicas of `nginx:alpine`, all running
`aurora-feed` publishes port `8090` to container port `80`
`http://localhost:8090` answers with the nginx page

solution: docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 || docker swarm init
missions.debrief: A service is a desired state, so swarm keeps replacing replicas until reality matches the number you declared. Pro tip: the published port works on every swarm node via the routing mesh, whichever node actually runs a replica.

missions.title: Change the Watch
missions.story:
Station chat, after the aurora page went white.

**Kip:** I pushed the new feed image to all three replicas at once and the whole page was down for forty seconds. Sorry!

**Ingrid:** Nobody does it that way again. One replica at a time, a short pause between each, and if the new version fails to come up, the old one goes back on its own. Engineer, roll `aurora-feed` onto `nginx:alpine` the proper way, and make those rules part of the service so they apply next time too.
objectives: Update the running service `aurora-feed` to the image `nginx:alpine`
Set the update parallelism to `1` and the update delay to `5s`
Set the update failure action to `rollback`
The service still has 3 running replicas and the update has completed
missions.startingState: A swarm is running with the service `aurora-feed` (3 replicas of `nginx:1.27-alpine`, port 8091). It has never been updated.
hints: A swarm service is replaced task by task. How fast, how many at once, and what happens on failure are properties of the service's update configuration, and they apply to this update and every later one.

Use `docker service update` on the existing service. Relevant flags: `--image`, `--update-parallelism N`, `--update-delay DURATION`, `--update-failure-action rollback`. `--detach=false` waits until the rollout finishes.

```bash
docker service update --detach=false \
  --image nginx:alpine \
  --update-parallelism 1 \
  --update-delay 5s \
  --update-failure-action rollback \
  aurora-feed

docker service inspect aurora-feed --pretty
```

commands: docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 || docker swarm init

validation.description: `aurora-feed` runs 3 replicas, all running `nginx:alpine`
The update parallelism of `aurora-feed` is `1`
The update delay of `aurora-feed` is `5s`
The update failure action of `aurora-feed` is `rollback`

params.command: for i in $(seq 14); do s=$(docker service inspect aurora-feed --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}'); [ "$s" = completed ] && break; sleep 1; done; echo $s

validation.description: The rolling update of `aurora-feed` has completed

solution: docker service update --detach=false --image nginx:alpine --update-parallelism 1 --update-delay 5s --update-failure-action rollback aurora-feed
missions.debrief: Swarm swapped the tasks one at a time, with a pause between them, so the feed never went fully dark, and a failed task would have triggered a rollback. Pro tip: `docker service rollback aurora-feed` undoes the last update by hand.

missions.title: Clearing the Snowdrifts
missions.story:
Ingrid's pre-winter checklist, last page:

`[ ] free disk space: the engine is at 94%`
`[ ] keep everything labelled keep=true (Tomasz's cores)`
`[ ] keep whatever is running or in use`

Tomasz has labelled the three things he cannot lose: a stopped container, a volume and an image, all `keep=true`. Everything else that nobody is using must go: stopped containers, unused volumes and dangling images. A bare `prune` would take his data with it, so use label filters.
objectives: Remove every stopped container except `keeper-log` (label `keep=true`)
Remove every unused volume except `ledger-vol` (label `keep=true`); `gauge-data` is in use and must stay
Remove every dangling image except the one labelled `keep=true`
Leave the running container `snow-gauge` and the tagged images `kestrel/drift:latest` and `kestrel/ledger-snap:latest` untouched
missions.startingState: Three throwaway stopped containers, two unused volumes and a few dangling images are mixed in with the things that must survive. A container `snow-gauge` is running and uses the volume `gauge-data`.
hints: Docker has a `prune` command for each kind of object. Pruning removes only what is unused, and most prune commands accept filters, so you can exclude anything carrying a particular label.

Try `docker container prune`, `docker volume prune` and `docker image prune`, each with `-f` and `--filter "label!=keep=true"`. Since Docker 23, `volume prune` skips named volumes unless you add `--all` (`-a`). Check with `docker ps -a`, `docker volume ls` and `docker images -f dangling=true`.

```bash
docker container prune -f --filter "label!=keep=true"
docker volume prune -af --filter "label!=keep=true"
docker image prune -f --filter "label!=keep=true"

docker ps -a
docker volume ls
docker images -f dangling=true
```

commands: docker run -d --name snow-gauge -v gauge-data:/data alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
for i in 1 2 3; do docker run --name drift-$i alpine:3.20 true; done
docker run --name keeper-log --label keep=true alpine:3.20 true
for v in 1 2; do printf "FROM alpine:3.20\nRUN echo snow-$v > /marker\n" | docker build -q -f - . ; done
printf 'FROM alpine:3.20\nRUN echo drift-tag > /marker\n' | docker build -q -t kestrel/drift:latest -f - .

printf 'FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL keep=true
RUN echo ledger-old > /marker
' | docker build -q -f - .

printf 'FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL keep=true
RUN echo ledger-tag > /marker
' | docker build -q -t kestrel/ledger-snap:latest -f - .

validation.description: Only `keeper-log` remains among the stopped containers
The running container `snow-gauge` is untouched
Only the volumes `gauge-data` and `ledger-vol` remain

params.command: echo "$(docker images -f dangling=true -q | wc -l | tr -d ' ')/$(docker images -f dangling=true -f label=keep=true -q | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"

validation.description: Exactly one dangling image remains, and it is the one labelled `keep=true`
The tagged image `kestrel/drift:latest` still exists
The tagged image `kestrel/ledger-snap:latest` still exists

missions.debrief: Each `prune` removes only what is unused, and `--filter label!=...` lets you fence off whatever you labelled to protect. Pro tip: `--filter until=720h` limits a prune to objects older than 30 days, which makes a safe scheduled job.
